clips.text: The president spent all this time talking about what's happening in Ukraine, right?
He said Ukraine was mobilizing soldiers, taking people practically off the streets, like dogs. He used pretty harsh words.
Then he said they were throwing them into the fire, using them as expendable material, and so on.
And a significant part of his speech was devoted to all these issues surrounding Ukraine.
As a citizen of the Russian Federation, I'll be honest with you:
I wasn't interested in a history lesson about whose land it is or isn't. It's a matter of debate, and now isn't the time for it.
Zelensky is ready to concede territory. De facto, it's Ukraine's, like it or not.
And Zelensky, despite my dislike for the man who put me under Ukrainian sanctions—I have no love for Zelensky—
but it's completely... I mean, I understand what he means.
He's prepared to give up part of Ukraine's territory in exchange for some kind of agreement to end the war.
I understand his logic.
Why start telling us that it's already our territory anyway?
Why say we're two brotherly peoples, that genetic studies confirm it? Well, yes, we're two brotherly peoples.
But we all descended from Adam and Eve, from the first people on Earth.
We're all related—distantly, very distantly, but related.
By that logic, you could say that too.
In church they say, brothers and sisters.
Before God there is neither Greek nor Roman.
Let's remember the Holy Scriptures. If Putin is a believer, surely he remembers that phrase.
So why say in this speech that we're brothers? Yes, but it has nothing to do with the matter at hand.
Why say it?
I want to hear our position in these negotiations,
not a history lesson or a discussion of how they're recruiting for the Ukrainian army.
And if we're going to talk about that, let's remember Pushilin's mobilization here—how they recruited students, young men from Donetsk, twenty to twenty-five, nineteen to twenty-five.
Why doesn't Putin talk about that?
How they were called up for supposed military training just before the special military operation, and then suddenly, bang—the war began. And where did they all end up?
Come on, let's talk about that.
Let's talk about recruitment from prisons. A few years ago, before the special military operation,
remember how our propagandists kept pointing at the Ukrainian armed forces, saying, 'Look, look how bad things are for them!'
'They're already recruiting people from prisons.'
'They've got no army left. They're taking criminals into the army.'
And us now? Forgive me, but here's an impertinent question.
My son went into the army from prison and ended up there, so to speak.
I'm not going to reveal all the details on air, but he came from prison.
And there are tens of thousands like him there. Not hundreds—tens of thousands. Tens of thousands.
How they're treated at the front—you don't need to tell me, respected, or not-so-respected, Mr. President.
I know how people who went from prison to the special military operation are treated.
And I know how long they survive on average at the front, including from officers' accounts—the average life expectancy of a prisoner in the zone of the special military operation.
Doesn't that happen here?
Where did the expression 'meat assaults' come from?
Where did it come from?
Did it come to us from Ukraine, 'meat assaults'?
No. That's our Russian invention, so to speak—forgive the dark, the dark irony.
It was here. It was our soldiers
who were sent into frontal attacks
by particularly outstanding generals like Lapin,
who was later named a Hero of Russia,
and was the face of United Russia in the recent, so-called elections,
if you can even call the whole thing an election.
Remember how he tried to cross that river several times?
Even Kadyrov called him out.
Officers privately questioned his ability to command, too.
Was he held accountable?
For the deaths, for the deaths of a huge number of people,
and for the equipment that was lost and burned?
How could he cross a river in the same spot
when the enemy had that spot zeroed in?
They crossed once, and were beaten back.
It was zeroed in, yet they crossed again.
And then they went a third time.
Did he answer for it? No.
So why tell me now that Ukrainians are being sent to the front as expendable material?
Is it any different here?
Look, respected—or not-so-respected—Mr. President,
at the internet you are slowing down, at that very same YouTube.
Just look up videos from the other side, posted by Ukrainian army units.
See what the war actually looks like.
And then do not tell us that things are somehow different on our side.
Remember Yegor Letov?
I am sure it is the same for them, and everything is going according to plan.
That is what is really happening, as I see it.
Everything is going according to plan.
The only question is: whose plan is it going according to? Is this how it is supposed to be?
More than a million. More than a million.
Yesterday I was with some Serbian friends. We sat and talked.
Remarkable people, with a remarkable love for us Russians, and enormous pain in their hearts
over what is happening.
They really... I saw it in their eyes.
Tears were welling up in their eyes as we talked, and when I
told them that, by our journalistic estimates, based on indirect evidence,
these are not proven figures, of course, just rough estimates,
more than a million people have been killed, wounded, or gone missing on both sides.
And the overwhelming majority of those killed, wounded, or missing
are Russians. Russians are dying on both sides!
Putin can say whatever he wants about history, referendums, or anything else,
but the fact is that Russians are dying today.
The total number of people killed in the special military operation is already greater than the losses during the Civil War.
During the Civil War, I mean at the front,
not those who died of typhus or starvation.
Fewer people died at the front in the Civil War.
Killed, wounded, missing. Fewer.
By our rough estimates, based on indirect evidence,
than in the course of the special military operation, on both sides.
I want to emphasize that again: on both sides.
If Russians are dying, then what is the point of all this talk?
We simply need to stop the war.
It is the fifth year now.
How much longer will you keep pursuing the goals of the special military operation?
How many human lives are you prepared to give up?
Is anyone from your inner circle at the front?
My son is at the front.
I have the right to say this.
The one thing I told him when he ended up there was:
Do everything you can to keep blood off your hands.
Please, try.
I understand it is a war,
but I am asking you, please,
let your hands remain clean, if that is possible.
